scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The passacaglia originated in early 17th-century Spain as a strummed guitar interlude between songs or dances, with the name derived from 'pasar' (to pass) and 'calle' (street).
It was first documented in Italian sources in 1606 and later transformed by Girolamo Frescobaldi into a series of continuous variations over a bass ostinato.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Used for religious processions and theatrical interludes in the 17th century.
In modern Ecuador and Peru, it serves as a civic anthem and a celebratory marker of regional identity during anniversaries and carnivals.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: In the European Baroque tradition, it was a slow, solemn dance in triple meter.
In the Andean tradition, it is a lively, march-like dance performed in processions, often involving brass bands and communal movement through streets.
Watch for Processional March.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (3AICNrKts3A)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Street processions or human chains (Andean).
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is defined by a bass ostinato, usually four to eight bars long, which repeats while upper voices vary.
Instruments include guitar (early), organ, harpsichord, violin, and in the Andean tradition, brass bands, accordions, and percussion like bombos and redoblantes.
Listen for the Guitar, Organ, Brass band, Accordion.
The pulse is 3/4 (Baroque) or 2/4 (Andean)..
A repeating, foundational bass line provides the harmonic anchor for increasingly complex melodic variations or brass-led march themes.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Girolamo Frescobaldi, Johann Sebastian Bach, François Couperin, Johannes Brahms, Benjamin Britten, Dmitri Shostakovich, Anton Webern.
The European passacaglia (solemn, triple meter, variation form) contrasts with the Andean pasacalle (lively, 2/4 march, brass band instrumentation).
Derived from Spanish street guitar music; influenced the development of the chaconne and later 20th-century orchestral variation forms.

narration: passacaglia is sibling of chaconne: Often confused with the passacaglia; both use ostinato patterns and were historically linked.
passacaglia is variant of kalejira: A Basque street-based social dance variant of the passacaglia.
